definition: Benefactor means a person who gives money or help to a person or cause.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word benefactor. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know benefactor should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A brass plaque in the lobby thanks the benefactor whose gift built the skating rink and whose visits kept it open.
A supporter is far weaker than a benefactor — a supporter may give nothing but applause, signing petitions and cheering from the sidelines, while a benefactor keeps the cause itself afloat.
A donor goes further than a supporter — money actually changes hands — but a single gift is enough to be a donor, while a benefactor keeps a person or cause afloat.

A patron backs artists or institutions, usually with money and often expecting a little credit — the named gallery, the program note. A benefactor may want no billing at all: the word simply names the person whose money or help a cause could thank.

A philanthropist gives to better life for people in general — hospitals, scholarships, whole causes — and the word stays large in scale and public in feel. A benefactor can work at any scale and usually stands behind one person or cause: the student, the band, the rink that could thank him.
the receiver of the gift — the mirror image

Benefactor means a person who gives money or help to a person or cause.
The town band owned two dented trumpets until Mr.
Aoki retired from his orchard.
He bought the band a full set of instruments, then kept showing up — a benefactor who drove the tuba to away games, paid for repairs, and taught the youngest players to oil their valves.
Money was only half of what he gave.
Benefactor is the exact word for Mr.
Aoki, because a benefactor is a person who gives money or help to a person or cause — the definition holds both halves of what he did.
Donor is narrower: a donor writes the check, and one check is enough; a benefactor's support tends to keep arriving.
Benefactor names the person behind the giving.
Keep the family straight: benevolent describes the kindly disposition, largess and munificence describe the giving itself, and bequeath is how a benefactor gives one last time — through a will.
Use benefactor when you mean the human being a cause could thank.

Every January, the bursar's office posted the same short list: students whose spring tuition had, without explanation, been paid in full.
Tomas made the list his second year, when a warehouse injury had ended his night shifts and, he assumed, his degree.
He asked the bursar who had paid.
The office would say only that the same benefactor had been clearing two or three student accounts a year since 1998.
There was no plaque to thank, no name on any building, no speech at graduation to applaud.
Tomas graduated owing nothing, and began, quietly, to save toward a list of his own.
